author: Mantu Kumar Deka
headline: Senior Data Engineer at IBM | Ex-HCL | Ex-R1 RCM | Data Engineering | GCP | PySpark | Databricks | Airflow | Python | SQL| DBT
text:
NULLs are one of those things you don’t notice… until something breaks.
I’ve seen cases where:
totals were wrong
joins dropped data
dashboards showed weird numbers
and the root cause was just NULL handling not done properly.
So I put together a small PySpark cheat sheet that I actually use in day-to-day work 👇
1. Replace NULL (column level)
Use coalesce() when you want control
→ good for specific columns
2. Replace NULL (bulk)
Use fillna()
→ easiest way to clean multiple columns at once
3. Check NULLs
isNull() / isNotNull()
→ basic but very important while debugging
4. Avoid NULL in calculations
Always wrap with coalesce(col, 0)
→ avoids wrong sums and calculations
5. Count NULLs
count(*) - count(col)
→ quick way to understand missing data
6. Drop NULL rows
dropna()
→ use carefully (can remove a lot of data)
7. Replace dirty values
na.replace()
→ useful for things like "NA", "unknown"
8. Conditional handling
when().otherwise()
→ when business logic is involved
9. Safe division
handle divide by zero using when()
→ avoids runtime issues
10. NULL profiling
calculate % NULL per column
→ helps in data quality checks
One thing I learned the hard way:
handle NULLs early in the pipeline, not at the end.
Makes everything simpler — joins, aggregations, even debugging.
If you work with PySpark, this is something you’ll use almost every day.

headline: Certified SnowPro Advanced Data Engineer | 4+ Years in Snowflake, DataBricks, Informatica, SQL, Python, AWS S3, Airflow and DBT | Expertise in Data Warehousing, ETL Pipelines & Cloud Data Integration
text:
Day 3/30 – DBT vs ETL

Both move and transform data… 
But the approach makes all the difference.

🔹 ETL 
➡️ Extract → Transform → Load 
➡️ Transformations happen outside the warehouse 
➡️ More data movement, higher complexity

🔹 dbt (ELT)
➡️ Load → Transform inside warehouse 
➡️ SQL-based, modular, and scalable 
➡️ Faster, cheaper, and easier to maintain

💡 Simple way to remember: 
👉 ETL brings the data 
👉 dbt builds trust on top of it

Modern data stack = ETL + Warehouse + dbt + BI

If you're learning Data Engineering or Analytics… 
Understanding this shift is a game-changer.

author: Sumit Gupta 📊
headline: Data & AI Expert | 130K+ Community | Top 5 AI/B2B SaaS Creator | EB1A | GDE | Ex-Notion, Snowflake, Dropbox
text:
SQL handles thousands of rows. PySpark handles billions. Knowing both is no longer optional in 2026.

Because in modern data work, the question is not which tool to use. It is how fluently you can switch between them - depending on the scale, the stack, and the speed you need.

Here is the ultimate SQL vs PySpark cheat sheet 👇

✅ Select Columns
↳ SQL: SELECT name, salary FROM employees;
↳ PySpark: df.select("name", "salary")

✅ Filter Rows
↳ SQL: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > 80000;
↳ PySpark: df.filter(df.salary > 80000)

✅ Sort Data
↳ SQL: SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC;
↳ PySpark: df.orderBy(df.salary.desc())

✅ Group & Count
↳ SQL: SELECT department, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department;
↳ PySpark: df.groupBy("department").count()

✅ Group & Sum
↳ SQL: SELECT department, SUM(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department;
↳ PySpark: df.groupBy("department").sum("salary")

✅ Join Tables
↳ SQL: SELECT e.name, d.department_name FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id;
↳ PySpark: employees.join(departments, employees.dept_id == departments.id)

✅ Add New Column
↳ SQL: SELECT name, salary, salary * 0.10 AS bonus FROM employees;
↳ PySpark: df.withColumn("bonus", df.salary * 0.10)

The truth is - SQL gets you hired. Bilingual SQL + PySpark gets you promoted.
